title: The Rosenbergs
summary: Josh and Chuck (credited in the transcript as "iHeart Intro" for Chuck's lines) cover the Rosenberg espionage case: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, their Soviet spy ring, the atomic bomb secrets passed through David Greenglass, the 1950-51 arrests and trial, the death sentences, the last-minute appeals and the June 1953 executions, and the later release of the Venona cables. The episode opens with banter about "We Didn't Start the Fire" and Billy Joel, and closes with listener mail about Cole's Notes.
topics: Susie and the Banshees Strange Fruit

segments.title: Show open
segments.summary: Standard iHeart intro and show opening.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: The hosts joke about the We Didn't Start the Fire song and Billy Joel's music before turning to the Rosenbergs.

segments.title: Overview of the Rosenberg case
segments.summary: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were a married New York couple convicted of espionage in 1951 and executed. Historians dispute Ethel's guilt. Julius was a Soviet spy, and the couple were the only Cold War spies convicted and executed.

segments.title: Early lives and meeting
segments.summary: Ethel and Julius were both born in New York and attended Seward Park High School. They met at City College and became committed communists, meeting at a charity benefit for a union.

segments.title: Julius's early involvement and 1941 FBI loyalty meeting
segments.summary: Julius joined a Young Communist League affiliated group and trained as an electrical engineer. He was hired by the US Army Signal Corps. In 1941 he faced an FBI loyalty meeting and the case was dropped. The couple moved to Knickerbocker Village in 1942.

segments.title: How Julius became a spy
segments.summary: Accounts differ on how Julius started spying. Julius's own claim of framing is false. Hosts cite a Soviet agent introduction at a Labor Day rally and his anti-fascism motives.

segments.title: Passing weapons secrets and failed Pitt Machine business
segments.summary: Julius passed weapons information such as the proximity fuse to the Soviets, handled first by Semyonov then Feklisov. He recruited David Greenglass, and they started Pitt Machine Products, which failed by 1948 amid family tension.

segments.title: Family animosity and Ruth's accident
segments.summary: Tension grew between David and Julius over debts and business. In February 1950 David's wife Ruth was badly burned in an apartment fire.

segments.title: Klaus Fuchs, Venona cables, and David Greenglass's arrest
segments.summary: The case began in February 1950 with Klaus Fuchs's confession. Venona cables helped identify spies; Harry Gold led investigators to David Greenglass, who was arrested June 15, 1950 and confessed.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts take a break before continuing the story.

segments.title: Arrests of Julius and Ethel
segments.summary: The FBI questioned Julius in June 1950 and had enough to arrest him July 17. Ethel testified before a grand jury and was arrested August 11, 1950. Both were charged with conspiracy under the Espionage Act of 1917.

segments.title: Atomic secrets from Los Alamos and the Jell-O box plan
segments.summary: David Greenglass worked at Los Alamos on the Manhattan Project from August 1944. Ruth recruited him as a spy. Julius devised a plan B courier system using a torn Jell-O box as a recognition token; Harry Gold later used the matching half to contact David and Ruth. Gold paid $500.

segments.title: Later atomic information and the frying pan
segments.summary: In September 1945 David returned to New York and gave Julius more notes and a sketch of the bomb. Julius reportedly burned the notes in a frying pan and paid David $200.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts pause the episode with a break.

segments.title: David Greenglass's deal and false testimony against Ethel
segments.summary: David's attorney advised him to blame the Rosenbergs. David testified before the grand jury that Ethel was not involved, then at trial implicated her. In 2001 David admitted he lied about Ethel to protect his wife.

segments.title: Trial lawyers, judge, and jury
segments.summary: Julius and Ethel were tried with Morton Sobell. Their lawyers were Manny Block and Alexander Rosenberg. Prosecutor Irving Saypol and Judge Irving Kaufman were known for anti-communism. The jury had one Black man, one white woman, and no Jewish members.

segments.title: Trial witnesses and digressions
segments.summary: Witnesses included Max Elitcher, Lewis Abel, George Bernhard, Harry Gold, and Elizabeth Bentley. Julius's doctor said Julius asked about inoculations for Mexico. The hosts digress on Cole's Notes-style jokes and Sir Mix-a-Lot.

segments.title: Verdict and sentencing
segments.summary: The trial lasted three weeks; all three were found guilty in March 1951. Sobell got thirty years; the Rosenbergs got death sentences, the judge citing Korean War aggression.

segments.title: Appeals, public campaign, and the execution standoff
segments.summary: Manny Block's appeals and a National Guardian article drew international support, including from Picasso and Einstein. Officials reportedly offered clemency for names; the Rosenbergs refused, and they were executed.

segments.title: Execution timing and funeral
segments.summary: The execution was moved earlier to before the Sabbath. The Rosenbergs were put to death at 8 pm, and a June 1953 funeral in Brooklyn drew about ten thousand people. They were buried at Wellwood Jewish Cemetery.

segments.title: Sons and legacy
segments.summary: Their sons Michael and Robert were adopted by Anne and Abel Meeropol. Michael became an economist and Robert an attorney, and they worked to clear their parents' names. Venona cables released in the 1990s confirmed Julius's espionage.

segments.summary: Hosts reflect on the jokes in the episode.
